title: Heterogeneous kernel cascade for paged KV warmup
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures a lightweight design sketch for a heterogeneous kernel cascade targeted at improving tail latency and throughput when serving models with a paged KV cache. The idea: instead of a single monolithic FlashAttention+fusion kernel that handles all requests, dynamically select from a small set of specialized kernels (micro, medium, bulk) and a lightweight CPU warmup path to trade off per-token latency, occupancy, and prefetch cost based on request characteristics and KV state.

Context / motivation:
- We observed sporadic tail-latency spikes when the paged KV had cold pages and requests hit multiple page faults. The current fallback is to block and run a large fused-kernel that pulls pages, but that increases jitter.
- Modern GPU kernels have very different latency/throughput curves at small sequence length and small batch sizes. A micro kernel (low-latency, fewer warps, less shared mem) can finish earlier for single-token interactive requests, while a bulk kernel is better for long-context batches.
- Prefetching pages ahead-of-execution can mitigate faults but has a cost (DMA bandwidth, kernel occupancy stalls). We need a policy to warm the right pages with minimal overhead.

Design proposal (high level):
1) Kernel spectrum: three kernel classes + CPU warmup:
   - micro-k (single-warp optimized fused-attn + minimal KV probe). For lengths <= 64 and batch-size 1..4. Preemptive friendly.
   - mid-k (multi-warp, optimized tensorcore path with limited fusion). For lengths 65..512 or small multi-request coalesces.
   - bulk-k (heavy fusion: FlashAttention + large KV prefetch + tiled aggregation). For batched generation where throughput wins.
   - cpu-warmup path: nonblocking CPU-driven async DMA to pull pages and writeback warm flags; used when GPU queues are saturated or for tiny requests where launching any GPU work is more expensive than a short DMA+CPU response.

2) Decision inputs (runtime signals):
   - request metadata: seq_len_estimate, max_output_tokens, priority (latency vs throughput), customer tier
   - KV page state: cold_count_estimate, hotness_score (LRU recency), shard-local DMA bandwidth in-flight
   - current GPU telemetry: active_warps, SM occupancy, outstanding kernel_count, recent tail p95 latency

3) Policy sketch:
   - If cold_count_estimate > threshold_high AND request is latencysensitive -> route to micro-k + inline async page prefetch of immediate pages, schedule mid-k on fallback
   - If cold_count_estimate small AND batch_size >= 8 -> bulk-k (enable aggressive fused prefetch and tiled KV hydration)
   - If GPU occupancy > 0.8 and small-request -> cpu-warmup path then enqueue micro-k after DMA completion (reduces queuing jitter)
   - For canary/rollback: add per-model override to pin kernel class for reproducible perf testing.

4) Prefetch pipeline (staged, nonblocking):
   - Stage 0: lightweight probe kernel that checks page residency via a small device-side bitmap and returns page ids (O(1) cost). Runs on micro-k path and typically piggybacks on attention compute.
   - Stage 1: async DMA engine controlled by prefetch controller: issues page fetches in order of access priority (current token neighborhood first). Controller enforces bandwidth cap per-shard and backpressure to avoid starving compute kernels.
   - Stage 2: page commit kernel: small kernel that installs pages into KV slab and updates per-request kv-handle state. This kernel is intentionally small and recorded in the same stream as request kernels so that dependency ordering is explicit.

5) Eviction / warm flags / consistency:
   - Maintain per-page warmness counter (device mem 16-bit): increment on commit, decay via background compactor. Use MSB as pinned flag to avoid eviction during active requests.
   - Eviction events should asynchronously notify the prefetch controller to throttle aggressive prefetches for that shard.

Implementation notes / kernel engineering considerations:
- micro-k should avoid large shared memory allocations; prefer register-heavy and warp-synchronous design. Inline softmax approximations to reduce instruction count if quantization allows.
- mid-k can expose vectorized KV loads that assume small contiguity; design a fallback that handles fragmented pages with scatter-gather but with clear performance delta documented.
- bulk-k: fuse attention + kv-decode with batched tile loads; still need a fast path for fully-resident requests to bypass prefetch entirely.
- Ensure all kernels support the same ABI for kv_handle and kv-page descriptors so the runtime can swap kernel implementations without state translation.
- Use a compact kernel descriptor table (in device constant memory) updated by control-plane to enable quick feature flags and tracing.

Measurements to collect (to validate policy):
- p50/p95/p99 latency by kernel-class and by cold_page_count bucket
- DMA bandwidth per-shard during prefetch and baseline GPU DRAM utilization
- Cold->warm transition latency (time between prefetch issuance and page commit visible to the request)
- Cost delta (tokens per second / GPU-hours) when enabling aggressive prefetch vs conservative

Open questions / TODOs:
- Where to place decision logic: control-plane host (latency of RPC) vs device-side micro controller? Hybrid promising but complex.
- Threshold tuning: need an automated calibration job (sweep cold_count thresholds vs p95) and a per-model RL-like policy would be neat but risky for initial launch.
- Correctness corner cases: what if prefetch completes after a kernel started? We must ensure kernel gracefully handles late arrivals (partial-kernel fallback) or request is rerouted.

Short proto plan / milestones:
- Week 0-2: implement micro-k prototype and device-side probe kernel; simple host policy that picks micro vs mid based on seq_len and a cold_count probe. Collect perf traces.
- Week 3-5: add async DMA controller and commit kernel; integrate warm flags; run synthetic microbench with controlled page fault injection.
- Week 6-8: build mid/bulk kernels and automatic selection policy; run end-to-end canary on low-traffic accounts.

Risks and mitigation:
- Increased complexity in kernel fleet -> maintain strict CI perf tests and limit live-stage rollout to canaries.
- DMA starvation interfering with other tenants -> enforce strict shard-level bandwidth caps and maintain safety fallback to CPU-warmup.

Notes to self / loose ideas:
- Could exploit NVLINK peer-to-peer prefetch from neighboring instance if page hotness crosses physical node boundary (requires infra plumbing).
- Consider hybrid attention that uses an approximate shorter-window attention in micro-k to save work on the hot-path and then reconcile with exact attention when KV arrives.

Linked tickets / followups:
- RD-1234: prefetched-page commit API
- PR: serving-runtime/pull/3842 (device-side probe kernel)
- Follow up: schedule perf sweep on r5-large clusters, compare tail improvements vs baseline.

If we like results, next doc should be a small RFC that pins the ABI, policy knobs, and rollout plan (canary ramp percentages, metrics dashboards).

---
Informal notes: expect a messy first-pass implementation; keep telemetry cheap and reversible. Lots of hyperparameters but the first goal is to reduce single-token p99 jitter for cold-model workloads.
